questions.stem: A 27-year-old pregnant woman spent the day with her nephew at a family celebration. The following day he developed a widespread vesicular rash which was diagnosed as chickenpox (primary varicella-zoster virus infection). She contacted her obstetrician the same day concerned about the risks of chickenpox as she had never had this illness and had not been vaccinated. She was 34 weeks pregnant and had mild asthma.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Send serum for VZV IgG testing

questions.explanation: Send serum for VZV IgG testing The patient’s history suggests that she may be naïve to VZV infection, and therefore although she is in the 3rd trimester and the fetus is not at risk of congenital varicella syndrome, she is at risk of severe varicella disease if infection occurs. There is also a risk that delivery may occur around the time of clinical illness if she is infected, risking perinatal transmission to the neonate. As she has sought medical attention promptly following exposure, it is appropriate to assess her preexisting immunity by checking her VZV IgG status before ordering the administration of VZIG, which is effective if given within 10 days of exposure. Varicella vaccine is a live attenuated vaccine and therefore is not appropriate in pregnancy. Aciclovir/valaciclovir prophylaxis is also not recommended to avert clinical illness in pregnant women exposed to chickenpox.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 1 Q19

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man presented with a 48-hour history of rash. He had a background of polymyalgia rheumatica and was taking prednisolone 40 mg OD. The lesions first appeared over the left side of his face but had spread over the past 24 hours. On examination his temperature was 38.5°C. There were vesicular lesions over his face, torso, and limbs.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.explanation: VZV PCR of lesion This patient is relatively immunocompromised on long-term steroids. The distribution of rash suggests the possibility of herpes zoster, or shingles. Subsequent widespread development of vesicular lesions indicates the possibility of disseminated zoster. In the presence of clinical uncertainly, the most definitive investigation would be PCR of vesicular fluid to confirm virus.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 3 Q26

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman sought medical advice 48 hours after a significant chickenpox exposure. She was 32 weeks pregnant with no personal history of chickenpox. She had not received the varicella vaccine. Investigations: Varicella IgG negative. She was treated with VZV immunoglobulin (VZIG).
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate definition of her treatment?
questions.explanation: Passive immunization This is an example of passive immunization, that is, the induction of immunity by transfer of antibodies to the nonimmune host. Vaccine immunization describes a method of immunization; partial immunization occurs when a person becomes ill with an infection but is not susceptible to severe illness or death; natural immunization is induction of immunity in a host who is exposed to the live pathogen; active immunization is the induction of immunity by antigen exposure, usually by vaccination.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 5 Q45

questions.stem: A 5-year-old child was reviewed 24 hours after a significant chickenpox exposure. She had acute myeloid leukemia and was undergoing treatment. She had been treated with human varicella-zoster immunoglobulin (VZIG) 9 weeks previously after her varicellazoster virus (VZV) IgG was found to be negative after another significant chickenpox exposure.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate action?
questions.explanation: Recheck VZV IgG This is to assess her immune status and re-administer VZIG as soon as possible if found to be varicella susceptible. Where possible, immune status should be tested in immune compromised individuals prior to the administration of VZIG. VZIG offers no additional protection to individuals who have VZV antibody. Patients may still develop chickenpox, however, following administration of VZIG, and therefore advice to commence antivirals should lesions develop is essential. A proportion of patients will seroconvert in the absence of clinical disease. For this reason, repeat testing for immune status is indicated, as in this case. If an exposure occurs after 3 weeks a further dose of VZIG is required if the individual is still varicella susceptible.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 6 Q13

questions.stem: A 24-year-old pregnant woman attended her GP at 14/40 as her 2-year-old daughter had developed a rash and fever consistent with chickenpox that morning. She had been born and brought up in the UK. She was unsure of her varicella immune status.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Ask her to re-attend if a rash illness develops
Give her intramuscular varicella zoster immunoglobulin
Reassure her that she is likely to be immune

questions.explanation: Check her varicella-zoster IgG She may require VZIG to reduce the risk of severe maternal disease and to reduce the risk of fetal varicella syndrome, but as it is a human product and there is time, she should have her immunity checked first, as she may be immune already.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 7 Q45

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man sought medical help after learning that he had had a significant exposure to chickenpox 24 hours earlier. He had no personal history of chickenpox and had not received the varicella vaccine. He had a history of hypertension and diabetes, and was taking enalapril and metformin. He had no known drug allergies.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate action?
questions.explanation: Administer varicella vaccine The chickenpox (varicella) vaccine would be recommended for all healthy adults who are exposed to chickenpox and do not know their immune status. Reasons for this are twofold. There is some evidence that vaccine may be effective in preventing chickenpox if given within 3 days of exposure. It is also an opportunity to protect the patient against future varicella exposures if they do not contract chickenpox on this occasion, so should be given irrespective of the interval since exposure. Varicella-zoster immune globulin (VariZIG/VZIG) is recommended for susceptible pregnant women and immunosuppressed individuals who have had a significant exposure. Intravenous immune globulin is not recommended. Valaciclovir is not indicated as prophylaxis for healthy adults but could be used to protect immunosuppressed individuals. Measuring titers may not provide an answer in time to give the vaccine and is not considered cost effective.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 8 Q28

questions.question: Zostavax (live attenuated herpes zoster vaccine).
questions.question_raw: Zostavax

parts.text: What is the efficacy in preventing zoster?
At what age is it recommended?

State whether the vaccine is contraindicated in each of the following: (i) unknown serostatus or unknown history of varicella-zoster virus; (ii) steroids; (iii) hairy cell leukemia; (iv) chronic granulomatous disease; (v) chronic obstructive pulmonary disease on intermittent steroids.

parts_raw.text: A.  What is the efficacy in preventing zoster?
B.  At what age is it recommended?
C.  Contraindicated in or not for following: I. Unknown serostatus or history of vzv. Ii. Steroids. IIi. Hairy cell leukemia. Iv. CGD? V. COPD on intermittent steroids.

questions.model_answer:
a) In the Shingles Prevention Study (~38,500 adults >60 y), incidence of herpes zoster was 51% lower in vaccinees (5.4 vs 11.1 cases/1000 person-years) and incidence of postherpetic neuralgia 67% lower (0.5 vs 1.4/1000 person-years); overall burden of illness was also reduced. Efficacy against zoster incidence persists ~8 years, against burden of illness ~10 years, and is greater in the 60-69 y group than in those >=70 y.
b) Licensed at >=60 y (2006) and >=50 y (2011), but CDC/ACIP recommend it only for adults >=60 y because of waning protection; it is not indicated to treat established zoster or PHN. It has been superseded by the recombinant vaccine (Shingrix), recommended at >=50 y and preferred.
c) (i) Unknown serostatus/history - not a contraindication; serology need not be checked before giving zoster vaccine. (ii) Steroids - contraindicated only with high-dose systemic therapy (>=20 mg/day prednisone or >=2 mg/kg/day for >=14 days); defer until at least 1 month after stopping. (iii) Hairy cell leukemia - contraindicated (lymphoproliferative malignancy; live vaccine). (iv) Chronic granulomatous disease - not contraindicated; CGD is a phagocyte defect and only live bacterial vaccines (BCG, live typhoid) are contraindicated. (v) COPD on intermittent/inhaled or short-course steroids - not contraindicated.
questions.beyond_mandell: Contraindication specifics are not in the chapter: ACIP/PHAC Canadian Immunization Guide - live zoster vaccine is contraindicated in immunodeficiency and high-dose systemic steroids (>=20 mg/day prednisone or >=2 mg/kg/day for >=14 days), not in CGD or inhaled/short-course steroids.

cohort_answer.text:
Zostavax (live) – 51% reduction in risk of zoster, 67% reduction of PHN; Shingrix (recombinant, inactivated) - 91% at preventing shingles and 97% PHN
Zostavax 60 or older 1 dose SC; Shingrix 50 or older 2 doses IM
Unknown serostatus: Yes because no need to check status before giving but, needs varicella vaccine if not immune/didn't have natural disease; Steroids: Yes if on high dose and for longer than 14 days (delay 1month after d/c); Hairy cell leukemia: Yes; CGD: No (cannot give live bacterial vaccines to CGD); Copd on intermittent steroids: No. Stop antivirals 24 hours prior to giving vaccine. Wait 1 year after an episode of shingles before giving either vaccine (or receiving Zostavax, wait a year to get Shingrix). Shingrix not approved in immunocompromised population yet. Can give in pregnancy.

questions.model_answer: (1) Pregnancy (live attenuated Oka-strain vaccine; also avoid pregnancy for 1 month after). (2) Significant immunocompromise - congenital immunodeficiency, lymphoproliferative or other malignancy on chemotherapy, high-dose systemic corticosteroids, advanced HIV; vaccine-strain rash is frequent and can be severe in these hosts. questions.model_answer: (1) Herpes simplex virus (HSV-1 or HSV-2); (2) Varicella-zoster virus. Both are alphaherpesviruses and are morphologically identical on electron microscopy — all herpesviruses share a double-stranded DNA core, an icosahedral capsid of 162 capsomers, tegument, lipid envelope with surface glycoproteins, and a diameter of about 160 nm — so EM cannot distinguish them; typing requires PCR/culture.

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Presentation within 72 hours of rash onset (or later if new lesions are still forming), particularly in adults >50 y, in whom antivirals accelerate cutaneous healing and reduce acute neuritis. (2) Complicated or high-risk zoster: herpes zoster ophthalmicus (sight-threatening), disseminated/visceral zoster, or any immunocompromised host - treat regardless of time from onset (IV acyclovir 10 mg/kg q8h).
b) (1) Postherpetic neuralgia (25%-50% of patients >50 y). (2) Herpes zoster ophthalmicus with keratitis, iridocyclitis, secondary glaucoma or neuroparalytic keratitis. (3) Ramsay Hunt syndrome - geniculate ganglion involvement with ear pain and vesicles in the external auditory meatus, loss of taste on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, ipsilateral facial palsy. (4) Meningoencephalitis/encephalitis; also granulomatous cerebral angiitis causing ischemic stroke after zoster ophthalmicus, transverse myelitis, Guillain-Barre syndrome, and segmental motor paralysis from anterior horn cell involvement.
c) Live zoster vaccine (Zostavax): 51% reduction in zoster episodes and 67% reduction in postherpetic neuralgia. The recombinant adjuvanted vaccine (Shingrix), now preferred, gives ~91%-97% protection against zoster and ~89%-91% against PHN.

Immunocompromised host (even if >72hrs). Goals of antiviral therapy: lessen severity/duration of pain, promote faster healing, prevent new lesions, decrease viral shedding/transmission risk, prevent post herpetic neuralgia. Ramsay Hunt syndrome - triad of ipsilateral facial paralysis, ear pain+vesicles in auditory canal, loss of taste anterior 2/3 tongue; 4. Aseptic meningitis/encephalitis; 5. Transverse myelitis; 6. Peripheral motor neuropathy; 7. Stroke syndromes; 8. Bells palsy.

questions.model_answer:
a) Give VariZIG (varicella-zoster immune globulin) as post-exposure prophylaxis - she is a seronegative pregnant woman with a significant household exposure, which is an explicit VariZIG indication. Ideally within 96 hours of exposure, but it is still given up to 10 days to attenuate illness. Do NOT give varicella vaccine (live, contraindicated in pregnancy). Counsel about pneumonitis risk, which is particularly severe in the second and third trimesters, and advise her to report fever, cough or rash immediately.
b) Exposure: her son was infectious from ~2 days before his rash (March 25) until all lesions crusted (April 2). Incubation is 10-21 days, and a case is contagious from ~2 days before rash, i.e., from day 8 after exposure. First possible contagious day = 8 days after first exposure, March 25 + 8 = April 1. Last possible contagious day = 21 days after last exposure, April 2 + 21 = April 23. Circle April 1 and April 23 (with VariZIG, extend the outer limit to 28 days after last exposure, i.e., April 30).
c) Oral acyclovir 800 mg five times daily for 7 days, started within 24-72 hours of rash onset; switch to IV acyclovir 10 mg/kg q8h if pneumonitis, neurologic involvement or other complicated/severe disease develops.
questions.beyond_mandell: The 10-21 day incubation and the day 8-to-21 (28 post-VariZIG) exposure window are CDC/PHAC infection-control figures, not stated in this chapter slice.

questions.model_answer:
a) Shingrix - recombinant glycoprotein E subunit (non-live, inactivated); adjuvanted with AS01B (MPL + QS-21 in liposomes); 2 doses IM 2-6 months apart; efficacy 96.6%-97.4% against zoster in adults 50-69 years (91.3% in >=70 y) and 88.5%-91.2% against postherpetic neuralgia.
Zostavax II - live attenuated Oka/Merck strain, high titer (~19,400 PFU/dose); no adjuvant; 1 dose subcutaneously; efficacy ~51% against zoster and 67% against PHN, higher in the 60-69 y group than in those >=70 y, with waning after ~8 years.
ACIP recommends Shingrix at >=50 years and prefers it over Zostavax, including in prior Zostavax recipients - so this 60-year-old should receive Shingrix.
questions.beyond_mandell: The AS01B adjuvant composition and the 2-6 month IM dosing interval are from the product monograph/ACIP 2018; the chapter states only that Shingrix is adjuvanted and given as two doses.

cohort_answer.text:
SHINGRIX | Recombinant | Yes (AS01B) | 2 | >90%
ZOSTAVAX II | Live | None | 1 | 50%
Mechanism of Action of AS01B Adjuvant: AS01B adjuvant induces a local and transient activation of the innate immune system by two immune enhancers: MPL, which signals through Toll-like Receptor 4, and QS-21 signaling which involves activity of the NLRP3 inflammasome complex. These two agonists activate antigen presenting cells loaded with antigen in the draining lymph node that enables recruitment of naive CD4+ T cells. Both MPL and QS-21 are required to induce the maximal frequencies of gE-specific cytokine-producing CD4+ T cells and the highest titers of gE-specific antibodies.

questions.model_answer:

questions.model_answer:
a) Both are the same live attenuated Oka strain, but the zoster vaccine contains a far higher titre - about 19,400 PFU per dose versus 1350 PFU for monovalent varicella vaccine (9800 PFU for MMRV) - because a high titre is needed to boost waning cell-mediated immunity in older adults rather than to prime a naive host.
b) Varicella vaccine - two doses; she is susceptible and non-pregnant. Zoster vaccine is not indicated in a VZV-naive person.
c) Herpes zoster vaccine - he is VZV-immune and >=50 years; give recombinant zoster vaccine (Shingrix), 2 doses.

questions.question: Zostavax (live attenuated zoster vaccine).
questions.question_raw: Zostavax

parts.text: How much does it reduce the risk of shingles and postherpetic neuralgia?
What are the neurologic complications of zoster?

What are the neurologic complications of Zoster?

questions.model_answer:
a) In the Shingles Prevention Study, Zostavax reduced the incidence of herpes zoster by ~50% (5.4 vs 11.1 cases/1000 person-years) and reduced the incidence of postherpetic neuralgia by ~67% (0.5 vs 1.4 cases/1000 person-years). (By comparison, Shingrix efficacy was ~96.6-97.4% for zoster in ages 50-69 and PHN prevention ~88.5-91.2%.)
b) Neurologic complications of zoster: (1) postherpetic neuralgia; (2) herpes zoster ophthalmicus (with keratitis/sight threat) and Ramsay Hunt syndrome (geniculate ganglion); (3) meningoencephalitis/encephalitis; (4) granulomatous cerebral angiitis causing ischemic stroke (after zoster ophthalmicus); (5) myelitis, motor neuropathy from anterior horn involvement, and Guillain-Barre syndrome.
c) Indications for IV acyclovir (10 mg/kg q8h): immunocompromised host, organ-/sight-threatening or disseminated disease, CNS involvement (encephalitis/myelitis), and inability to tolerate or absorb oral therapy.

cohort_answer.text: A) Zostavax (live attenuated): reduces herpes zoster incidence by 51% and PHN incidence by 67% vs placebo. Shingrix (recombinant): 95% effective preventing herpes zoster, 90-100% effective reducing PHN, longer immunity. B) PHN (most common); herpes zoster ophthalmicus; CNS infection (meningitis, encephalitis); Ramsay-Hunt syndrome; acute retinal necrosis; myelitis, GBS; stroke-like syndrome (cerebral angiitis). C) Any organ-threatening disease; immunocompromise; unable to tolerate PO.

questions.model_answer:
a) Zostavax is a live attenuated (high-titer Oka, ~19,400 PFU/dose) vaccine; Shingrix is an adjuvanted, inactivated recombinant glycoprotein E subunit vaccine given as two doses. Shingrix is more efficacious and ACIP considers it preferable to Zostavax.
b) Zostavax: prevention of herpes zoster in immunocompetent adults (FDA-approved >=50, ACIP recommended >=60). Shingrix: prevention of herpes zoster in adults >=50, two doses, including previous recipients of Zostavax. Neither is indicated to treat established zoster or PHN.
c) Zostavax efficacy wanes with advanced age: it was more effective at preventing zoster in the younger elderly (60-69) than the older elderly (>=70), though it prevented PHN similarly in both groups. Shingrix retains high efficacy even at >=70 (91.3%), declining much less with age.

cohort_answer.text: A) Zostavax: live attenuated vaccine. Shingrix: inactivated (recombinant glycoprotein E vaccine with AS01B adjuvant). RZV superior to ZVL in reducing herpes zoster incidence and PHN in patients >60. B) Zostavax: immunocompetent patients ≥50 without contraindications when Shingrix contraindicated/unavailable; contraindications include immunosuppression, hypersensitivity history, pregnancy, precaution in breastfeeding. a) Congenital varicella syndrome is characterized by cicatricial skin scarring, hypoplastic (limb) extremities, eye abnormalities (cataracts, chorioretinitis, microphthalmia), and CNS impairment (cortical atrophy, seizures, intellectual disability); intrauterine growth restriction is also seen.

a) Determine her susceptibility (history of chickenpox/vaccination or serology). The son's infectious period ran from ~2 days before rash (March 25) until all lesions crusted; her exposure window is March 25 to about April 2. If she is seronegative and within 10 days of first significant exposure, give VariZIG as soon as possible (seronegative pregnant women with significant exposure should receive VariZIG).
b) If she remains well she is only potentially infectious during her own at-risk incubation window (~10-21 days after exposure, extended to day 28 if VariZIG was given); monitor for rash. She herself need be isolated only if she develops varicella (then until all lesions crust).
c) Treat with acyclovir, started as early as possible (ideally within 24-72 h of rash); pregnant women with varicella should be treated because of the risk of severe/pneumonitic disease in the second/third trimester. Use IV acyclovir 10 mg/kg q8h for severe disease or pneumonitis.

questions.model_answer:
a) Herpes zoster ophthalmicus (reactivation of VZV in the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal/fifth cranial nerve).
b) Two neurologic complications: (1) postherpetic neuralgia; (2) granulomatous cerebral angiitis with ischemic stroke (other options: acute retinal necrosis, encephalitis).
c) Herpes zoster ophthalmicus is zoster involving the first (ophthalmic) branch of the fifth cranial nerve, a sight-threatening condition. Vesicles on the tip/side of the nose (Hutchinson sign) suggest corneal involvement, though their absence does not guarantee corneal sparing. It can cause keratitis, which may be followed by severe iridocyclitis, secondary glaucoma, or neuroparalytic keratitis, risking vision loss. Ophthalmologic consultation should be obtained for any suspected case, with prompt antiviral therapy.

cohort_answer.text:
A: Herpes Zoster Ophthalmicus - reactivation of VZV within the trigeminal ganglion

B: Post-herpetic neuralgia. Acute retinal necrosis. (Additional neurological complications of Ramsay Hunt: Ipsilateral facial paralysis, Ipsilateral altered taste perception and tongue lesions, Hearing abnormalities, lacrimation, vestibular disturbances (vertigo). Additional neurological complications of VZV: Post-herpetic neuralgia, Acute retinal necrosis, Herpes zoster ophthalmicus, Ramsay Hunt syndrome, Aseptic meningitis, Encephalitis, Peripheral motor neuropathy, Myelitis, Guillain Barre syndrome, Stroke (VZV vasculopathy) - Moya moya, Cerebellitis)

C: Herpes zoster ophthalmicus - Herpes zoster involvement of the ophthalmic division of the fifth cranial nerve. HZO begins with a prodrome of headache, malaise, and fever. Unilateral pain or hypesthesia in the affected eye, forehead, and top of the head may precede or follow the prodrome. With the onset of the rash, hyperemic conjunctivitis, uveitis, episcleritis, and keratitis may occur; ptosis is rare. Acute keratitis typically involves the epithelial, stromal, or endothelial layers of the cornea. Patients who develop epithelial or stromal keratitis are most at risk for vision loss. Vesicular lesions on the side or tip of the nose correlate highly with eye involvement (Hutchinson's sign). Early diagnosis and treatment is critical to prevent progressive corneal involvement and potential loss of vision. Zoster sine herpete - severe ear pain and facial weakness without rash, very difficult to clinically distinguish from Bell's palsy; has been reported to comprise up to 30% of Ramsay Hunt cases

questions.model_answer:
a) Both are live attenuated Oka-strain vaccines, but Varivax is the low-titer varicella vaccine (~1350 PFU/dose monovalent) given to prevent chickenpox in the young/susceptible (from 12 months of age), whereas Zostavax is a high-titer (~19,400 PFU/dose) formulation designed to boost cell-mediated immunity and prevent herpes zoster in older adults (>=50/60).
b) 31M, non-immune, immunocompetent: varicella vaccine (Varivax), 2 doses.
c) 51M with previous chickenpox: zoster vaccine, Shingrix preferred (2 doses).
d) 63F with previous shingles: Shingrix (given >=50 including after a prior zoster episode), 2 doses.
e) Reasons Shingrix (recombinant adjuvanted) is better than Zostavax: (1) far higher efficacy (~97% vs ~50% for zoster; ~90% vs ~67% for PHN); (2) it is inactivated/non-live, so it can be used in immunocompromised hosts in whom the live vaccine is contraindicated; (3) more durable protection with less waning of efficacy with advancing age.
questions.beyond_mandell: The Shingrix immunocompromised indication and Varivax age-12-month/dosing schedule are ACIP/CDC recommendations; the chapter supports the efficacy figures, live-vs-recombinant distinction, and PFU titers.

cohort_answer.text: Difference: Varivax given >12 months of age; Zostavax for age >50. Reasons Shingrix (recombinant zoster) better: better immunogenicity (>90% effective vs 50%); safer; can use in immunocompromised host. Indications: age >50 who previously received Zostavax or had HZ (after at least 1 year); >18y at increased HZ risk due to immunodeficiency/immunosuppression.

questions.model_answer:
a) Confirm the diagnosis in the room-mate; isolate the room-mate (airborne + contact). This patient is <24 months post-BMT and remains at high risk, so give VariZIG as soon as possible, up to 10 days after exposure, regardless of prior serostatus. Consider pre-emptive valacyclovir/acyclovir if VariZIG is unavailable; place in airborne isolation during the at-risk window and treat with IV acyclovir if varicella develops. If she becomes infected, she is contagious from ~1-2 days before rash until all lesions have crusted.
b) At 12 months post-BMT (well, not immunosuppressed) give inactivated vaccines per the reconstitution schedule: pneumococcal conjugate series, Hib, tetanus/diphtheria (DTaP/Tdap), inactivated polio, hepatitis B, meningococcal, HPV, and inactivated influenza. c) Live attenuated varicella/zoster vaccine may be given only >=24 months post-transplant and only if the patient is immunocompetent and free of active GVHD/immunosuppression. Two contraindications at that time: (1) ongoing immunosuppression or active graft-versus-host disease; (2) recent immune globulin/VariZIG or IVIG administration (defer live vaccine), or a hypersensitivity reaction to a vaccine component.
questions.beyond_mandell: Post-HCT vaccine reconstitution schedule and the 24-month live-vaccine deferral are IDSA/CDC/Red Book transplant guidance; this chapter states only that VZV vaccine is a live vaccine and confirms VariZIG use in exposed immunocompromised persons.

cohort_answer.text: A) Confirm diagnosis; incubation 14-16 days (range 10-21); infectivity 24-48h pre-exanthem until all lesions crusted (day 8-21 post-exposure isolation, 28 if VZIG used); confirm vaccine/infection/serologic status; VZV-seronegative HCT recipients transplanted within previous 24 months (or >24 months if continued immunosuppression e.g. chronic GVHD) should get VariZIG within 10 days of contact; seropositive but highly immunosuppressed patients should also get VariZIG; cannot give vaccine post-BMT until at least 2 years; isolate roommate in airborne; isolate BMT patient in airborne from day 8 post-exposure until day 28 (VZIG given). B) Immunize with 2 doses of Shingrix at least 1 year after herpes zoster episode; other vaccines 12 months post-BMT include 3 doses PCV at 3-6 months then PPV-23 at 12-18 months, HiB conjugate 3 doses at 6 months, Td at 6 months, inactivated polio at 6 months, HepB 3 doses at 6 months, HPV 3 doses at 6 months, meningococcal at 6 months, influenza 4-6 months post-transplant; live vaccines (MMR, varicella, YF) at 24 months post-BMT. C) Live attenuated Zostavax: wait 24 months post-transplant; inactivated Shingrix: wait 3-6 months post-transplant. Contraindications: hypersensitivity reaction; ongoing immunosuppression (for GVHD); IVIG (last 8-11 months).

parts.text: Measles.
Measles vaccine.
Varicella.

parts_raw.text: A) Measles
B) Measles vaccine
C) Varicella

questions.model_answer:
a) Measles (wild-type): no defined congenital malformation syndrome; associated with spontaneous abortion, premature delivery and stillbirth, and congenital measles (rash) if maternal infection is near delivery.
b) Measles vaccine: live vaccine is contraindicated in pregnancy, but no congenital anomalies have been documented from inadvertent vaccination - it is not an indication for termination.
c) Varicella: congenital varicella syndrome - cicatricial skin lesions, limb hypoplasia, ocular defects (chorioretinitis, cataracts, microphthalmia) and CNS abnormalities (cortical atrophy, seizures, intellectual disability).
questions.beyond_mandell: The absence of documented defects after inadvertent measles vaccination (NACI/ACIP) and the varicella syndrome features are outside this chapter.
